pages.text: Abeiku was watching hens scratch in his grandmother’s yard when his cousin Naomi said something odd. ‘Did you know a hen is a kind of dinosaur?’ Abeiku laughed. ‘A dinosaur? It cannot even fly over the fence.’
sentences: Abeiku was watching hens scratch in his grandmother’s yard when his cousin Naomi said something odd.
‘Did you know a hen is a kind of dinosaur?’ Abeiku laughed.
‘A dinosaur?
It cannot even fly over the fence.’
pages.alt: A boy laughs at a hen while a girl looks serious in a village yard.

pages.text: Next day they asked Madam Quansah. She did not say yes or no. ‘First, find out how long ago dinosaurs lived,’ she said. She gave them a 150 m rope with a knot at every metre. ‘One metre is one million years. You are standing at today.’
sentences: Next day they asked Madam Quansah.
She did not say yes or no.
‘First, find out how long ago dinosaurs lived,’ she said.
She gave them a 150 m rope with a knot at every metre.
‘One metre is one million years.
You are standing at today.’
pages.alt: A teacher gives two children a long knotted rope on a school field.

pages.text: They placed a pin 30 cm from the start for our species, Homo sapiens, about 300,000 years old. At just over one metre they set a pebble for the Lake Bosumtwi crater, about 1.07 million years old. ‘Everything we know about people fits in the first step,’ said Abeiku.
sentences: They placed a pin 30 cm from the start for our species, Homo sapiens, about 300,000 years old.
At just over one metre they set a pebble for the Lake Bosumtwi crater, about 1.07 million years old.
‘Everything we know about people fits in the first step,’ said Abeiku.
pages.alt: Two children place a pin and a pebble along a rope near the start.

pages.text: They kept walking. At 66 m, Naomi stopped. ‘This is the big extinction,’ she read, ‘about 66 million years ago, when an enormous asteroid struck and every dinosaur except the birds died out.’ Abeiku looked back at the tiny start. ‘We walked sixty-six steps, and people are only at the beginning.’
sentences: They kept walking.
At 66 m, Naomi stopped.
‘This is the big extinction,’ she read, ‘about 66 million years ago, when an enormous asteroid struck and every dinosaur except the birds died out.’ Abeiku looked back at the tiny start.
‘We walked sixty-six steps, and people are only at the beginning.’
pages.alt: Two children stand at a marker with a picture of an asteroid in the sky.

pages.text: At 135 m they reached the end of the rope. ‘A plant-eating dinosaur called Jobaria lived in what is now Niger, in West Africa, about 135 million years ago,’ read Naomi. ‘That is the same part of Africa as Ghana,’ said Abeiku. ‘But 135 steps back in time.’
sentences: At 135 m they reached the end of the rope.
‘A plant-eating dinosaur called Jobaria lived in what is now Niger, in West Africa, about 135 million years ago,’ read Naomi.
‘That is the same part of Africa as Ghana,’ said Abeiku.
‘But 135 steps back in time.’
pages.alt: The children stand at the end of the rope with a picture of a long-necked dinosaur.

pages.text: They read more. Scientists found about 50 Jobaria specimens at one site, apparently after a flash flood. And the first Spinosaurus bones, found in Egypt in 1912, were destroyed in a bombing raid in 1944, so for years scientists had only drawings and photographs. ‘Fossils are fragile,’ said Naomi. ‘And so is the evidence.’
sentences: They read more.
Scientists found about 50 Jobaria specimens at one site, apparently after a flash flood.
And the first Spinosaurus bones, found in Egypt in 1912, were destroyed in a bombing raid in 1944, so for years scientists had only drawings and photographs.
‘Fossils are fragile,’ said Naomi.
‘And so is the evidence.’
pages.alt: The children look at an old drawing of a dinosaur skeleton and a photograph of bones.

pages.text: Back at school, Madam Quansah put two skeletons side by side: a meat-eating theropod dinosaur and a chicken. Abeiku counted: legs like a bird’s, three toes pointing forward, a wishbone. ‘Birds come from the theropods,’ she said. ‘They are living dinosaurs.’ Abeiku looked at the hen. The hen looked back.
sentences: Back at school, Madam Quansah put two skeletons side by side: a meat-eating theropod dinosaur and a chicken.
Abeiku counted: legs like a bird’s, three toes pointing forward, a wishbone.
‘Birds come from the theropods,’ she said.
‘They are living dinosaurs.’ Abeiku looked at the hen.
The hen looked back.
pages.alt: A teacher shows two skeleton drawings, one dinosaur and one chicken, to the children.

pages.text: They left a stone at the 66 m knot with a card: ‘The hen’s family line goes back past this stone. And we do not know everything, because new fossils are still being found.’ Abeiku scattered some grain for the hen. ‘Thank you, little dinosaur,’ he said. The end.

And we do not know everything, because new fossils are still being found.’ Abeiku scattered some grain for the hen.

activities.question: On the children’s rope, what does one metre stand for?

activities.prompt: Predict: where on the rope will dinosaurs go, if people are 30 cm from the start?

activities.question: How far from the start was the big extinction on the rope?

activities.definition: A rocky object that travels around the Sun, much smaller than a planet.

activities.question: Why did Naomi say “the evidence is fragile”?
options: Fossils can be lost or destroyed, so scientists may only have photos or drawings

activities.question: Which living animals are descended from theropod dinosaurs?

activities.prompt: Put these in order from most recent to longest ago.
items: Lake Bosumtwi crater forms (about 1.07 million years ago).
The big extinction (about 66 million years ago).
Jobaria lives in Niger (about 135 million years ago).

activities.prompt: Abeiku first laughed at the idea that a hen is a dinosaur, then changed his mind. How does it feel to change your mind because of evidence?
